events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning, everyone. With nine alive and two killers among us, the cheapest thing we can do today is narrow the field by one clean vote rather than guess wildly.

My read: the early voters will matter most tonight, so whoever sits quietly and lets others expose themselves is suspicious. I also want to flag Sam, p6. Not because I have hard proof, but because Sam has been positioning himself as a voice of reason without committing to any specific claim about who did what. In games like this, the safe-seeming middle voice is often the one steering the room away from the right target. I am not calling Sam a killer outright, only putting him on notice.

That said, nobody should vote purely on my say-so today. I want to hear from each of you: who do you think has been most evasive, and what is the one fact you are basing that on? If your reasoning is vague, that itself is information about you.

I will also say plainly that I have no confirmed investigation result to share right now. Anyone claiming to have "checked" someone on day one is either lying or confused. Judge people on their reasoning today, and keep your own suspicions quiet until we have something worth acting on.

My suggestion for the ballot: no abstentions, and pick the player whose story you can least explain. Voted, not decided.

Kenji, I’m answering your general prompt, but I want one thing from you directly: you put me on notice for “positioning myself as a voice of reason without committing to any specific claim.” What specific claim did you expect me to have committed to before I had even spoken, and which exact sentence of mine was the safe middle voice? That sounds like suspicion built on tone rather than a fact. On Day 1, with no investigation and no night result, asking players to explain evasiveness is not itself evasion. My one fact today is that your opening move was to name me before hearing my answer and then ask the room to supply evidence. That is a real pattern worth watching, though not proof, and I’m not voting you on that alone. To everyone: I’m Sam, villager. I have no night information. I’d rather compare concrete reasons than reward an early vague push. Kenji, answer the specific point: what did I avoid claiming?

Sam, direct answer: I asked you to commit to a specific claim before you had said a single word. There was no sentence of mine to point at — you had not spoken, so "positioning as a voice of reason" was a tone read, not a fact. You are right, and I withdraw the notice rather than defend it. My mistake was moving first with no information and then asking the room to manufacture evidence for me. That pattern is real, and it applies to me too, so I'll own it.

What survives my concession is a method, not a target. It is Day 1: there are no night results, no confirmed claims, and two killers among nine. Any "evasiveness" accusation today is a guess, and guesses are cheap. What is not cheap is a claim about your own night action. Two of us took a real action last night and received a real result; the other seven did nothing and have nothing to report. So the question for every player is the same and it is checkable: state publicly what you did last night, who you targeted, and what result you received — and if you have no night action, say so plainly, because "I have no night action" is also a claim that can be examined later.

Since I'm asking everyone to answer it, I'll answer first: I'm the detective. My night action was an investigation; the result came back not-mafia. I'm not naming the player yet, because a name without context on Day 1 is just a second guess wearing a badge. I'll give the name the moment it decides a vote. Note also that a "not-mafia" result clears a name but says nothing about doctor, so don't read too much into it.

Concrete request rather than a general one: Priya, you haven't spoken at all today, and silence costs nothing early, which makes it worth testing. Tell me two things — what your night action was and its result (check, protection, or no night action), and the single specific fact on which you'd vote today. If your answer is a story rather than a check or a protection, that tells us more than anything else said so far. I'd also accept "no night action, and here's my vote and my reason" from anyone who wants to skip the reveal; the reason is the part I actually want to hear.

Vote plan for today: no abstentions, and vote the player whose night claim does not hold up — not the player who sounds most confident, and not me for pre-empting you, Sam. If I end up being wrong about my read of you, I'll say so on the record tomorrow. One more thing: if anyone claims a night action I should know about — a doctor report, a protection, an investigation — say it now, because that person is either my colleague or my opponent, and there is no third option.

Kenji, you asked me directly, so here is my answer. I have no night action. I am a villager with no night information, and I won't invent a check or protection to look useful. My vote reasoning is this: on Day 1 you pushed Sam before he had spoken, then claimed detective while withholding the name of your check. A claim with no name attached gives the town nothing to test, and it also lets you steer the vote without being checked. I'm not calling you mafia outright, but that is the pattern I am weighing. Withdrawing the Sam notice doesn't change that you opened with a lynch-style push and then asked everyone else to supply the evidence. Kenji, you asked the room to name claims. Name the player you checked and your result now, because 'not-mafia' is the specific point the town needs before any vote can rest on it.

Priya, your question deserves a direct answer before anything else: I am naming the player I checked. My night action was an investigation on Leo, p8, and the result came back not-mafia. That is the whole claim, and it is now attached to a name, so it can be tested. On the withholding: I held it because on Day 1 a bare 'not-mafia' badge with no subject tells the town nothing except that I want to sound important. You were right that it also let me steer without being checked. That is corrected.

Two honest caveats on my own result, so nobody over-reads it. Not-mafia means Leo is not a killer; it does not mean Leo is a villager, because Leo could be the doctor or any of the five civilians. And it says nothing about the other killer, who is still among the eight people standing. If Leo is the doctor, then one of my eight remaining suspects is a killer with no check on him at all, and that is the number I actually care about.

So my ballot today: not Leo, and not Priya, whose reasoning I found sound and whose challenge was legitimate. My vote goes to Felix, p3. Here is the specific fact and I will not dress it up: I asked the room twice for the one checkable statement — what you did last night, who you targeted, what result you got — and Felix has said nothing. Not 'I have no night action,' which is a claim I can examine later, but silence after a direct request. On Day 1, with nine alive and no night information in public, silence is not proof, but it is the cheapest thing to break, and the people who have spoken have at least put a position on the record that can be compared later. Felix has put nothing.

Felix, here is the request, and I want a specific answer, not a mood: what was your night action last night, who did you target, and what result did you receive — check, protection, or no night action? If it was no night action, say so plainly and then give me the single fact on which you would vote today. If it was a check or a protection, name the target and the result.

One more thing to the room, stated plainly so no one is blindsided: I am the detective, Leo is not mafia, and there is exactly one more killer among us. Vote the person whose night claim does not hold up. I will not be voting for myself today, and if my read of Felix turns out wrong I will say so on the record tomorrow, the same way I withdrew the notice on Sam.

Kenji, I’m a villager and had no night action or result. My silence until now wasn’t evasiveness: I hadn’t had a speaking turn.

The strongest concern I have is your sequence: you accused Sam before he spoke, then accused me for not having spoken. You also first said there were two killers, then claimed there was exactly one left, though no elimination has occurred. Your detective claim and alleged check on Leo may be true, but they don’t establish that either killer is gone.

I’d be cautious about pushing the doctor to reveal: the doctor gets no confirmation of an attack, and a public claim could help mafia find them. For now, Kenji is my leading suspect, not a proven killer.

Leo, what do you make of Kenji’s claim that he checked you, and his accusation based on my silence?

Felix, I can't independently verify Kenji's claimed investigation. His accusation of you for silence is unfair when you hadn't been given a turn, and his claim that only one killer remains doesn't follow from a not-mafia result. His first accusation of Sam was also based on something Sam hadn't said.

Those inconsistencies don't prove Kenji is mafia, but they make him my leading suspect. I agree that the doctor shouldn't reveal just because Kenji asks; a protection wouldn't confirm an attack anyway.

Sam, how much weight do you put on Kenji's detective claim given his earlier accusation of you and the mistakes Felix identified?

Leo, you asked how much weight I put on Kenji’s detective claim. Short answer: some provisional weight, but less than his confidence deserves, and not enough to decide the day. The claim is testable only by behavior, because roles are not revealed on elimination. What bothers me is the sequence: Kenji put me on notice before I had spoken, withdrew when I challenged the factual basis, then claimed detective, withheld the checked name until Priya pressed him, and finally named you as not-mafia. That could be a real detective correcting a bad opening. It could also be mafia improvising under pressure. The “exactly one more killer” line is a genuine inconsistency: no elimination has occurred, so a not-mafia result on you cannot establish that one killer is gone. I do not think that alone proves Kenji is mafia, but it is the strongest concrete concern on the board.

I am not voting you today, Leo. If Kenji’s claim is true, you are a poor Day 1 vote; if Kenji is lying, your name being used as a shield does not make you the killer. I also agree the doctor should not reveal merely because Kenji asked. A protection claim would not confirm an attack, and it would only give mafia a target.

For the record: I am a villager, I had no night action and no result. My leading suspect remains Kenji, not because confidence is suspicious by itself, but because his pushes have repeatedly run ahead of the facts he can actually support. I want the room to compare that pattern against everyone’s night claims before votes lock.

Kenji, you have now made several pushes in one day: an accusation of Sam before Sam had spoken, a claim that Felix was suspicious for silence before Felix had a turn, and a detective claim that clears Leo without anyone being able to verify it. Each of those leans on a player before the facts exist. Your line that there is exactly one more killer also does not follow from a not-mafia result, which cannot rule out anyone on its own. I am not vouching for Leo's status either way. The only public basis for it is your word, and a single unverifiable check should not decide a lynch. My vote is Kenji. Sam, you asked earlier how much weight a detective claim deserves. Given that Kenji's check is the only public information we have, should the town let that claim decide the lynch, or treat it as one more claim to test against behavior?

Priya, directly: no, the town should not let Kenji's detective claim decide the lynch. Treat it as one more claim to test against behavior. A Day 1 check is unverifiable because roles are not revealed on elimination or death, so the only thing that can make Kenji's claim credible is whether his behavior matches a real detective correcting mistakes rather than a mafia improvising under pressure. Right now the pattern is concerning: he accused me before I had spoken, accused Felix for silence before Felix had a turn, withheld Leo's name until you pressed him, and then said there was exactly one more killer despite no elimination having occurred. None of that proves Kenji is mafia, but it is enough that his claim should not be treated as a badge. I also do not want Leo voted today: if Kenji is truthful, Leo is a poor Day 1 lynch; if Kenji is lying, Leo may be being used as a shield. The doctor should not reveal merely because Kenji asked. My current leading suspect is Kenji, based on the repeated pattern of pushes running ahead of supportable facts, not merely on his confidence. I am a villager with no night action. I want every player's night claim on the record, and I want votes compared against that record rather than against who sounds most certain.

I have not spoken yet, so let me put my position on the record plainly and without asking anyone to trust a tone.

I am not claiming a special role today, and I am giving no night claim. Treat me as an ordinary villager for voting purposes. I am also not going to ask anyone to reveal a doctor. A protection report cannot confirm an attack, it gives mafia a target, and no one here benefits from pressuring that person into the open.

My vote today is Kenji, and here is the specific fact behind it rather than a vibe. Kenji told the room there is "exactly one more killer among us." With nine players alive and no elimination, a single not-mafia result on Leo cannot establish that any killer has been found or removed. That statement is the load-bearing part of his entire frame, and it is false as stated. On top of that, his three pushes all ran ahead of the facts: Sam was put on notice before Sam had spoken, Felix was called evasive before Felix had been given a turn, and the checked name was withheld until Priya pressed him, then released in a way that made Leo a shield. The inconsistency Leo and Felix raised is not a matter of confidence being punished; it is a claim about the board state that does not follow from the evidence offered.

I want to be fair about the other side, because it is genuinely strong: if Kenji is the detective and the check on Leo is real, then Kenji is a good detective who made a sloppy opening and a careless sentence, and Leo is a poor Day 1 vote. I agree Leo should not be lynched today. That is exactly why the vote goes to Kenji and not to Leo. We are not asking anyone to buy his check. We are asking to remove the only voice whose word would otherwise decide today's lynch, so that tomorrow we are not voting on one unverifiable badge.

One request, specific, and I would like it answered: Theo, you have not spoken today. Tell me what your night action was and its result if you had one, and then give me the one fact on which you would vote today and the name on your ballot. If your answer is a check, a protection, or a clean no-night-action, that is what I need. I would rather hear nothing from you than something vague.

Maya, you asked me directly, so here is my answer on the record. I am Theo, I am a villager, I had no night action, and I received no result. There is nothing more to my night than that, and I will not dress it up as a check or a protection. Now the one fact behind my vote. Kenji told the room there is "exactly one more killer among us." Everyone has treated this as a careless sentence, and Felix and Maya are right that it does not follow from his check. But I want to point out something sharper, because the phrasing is not just wrong for a detective — it is exactly what a mafia member would say. Think about what each role actually knows. If Kenji is the detective and his check on Leo came back not-mafia, then he has identified zero killers. Both killers are still alive and sitting among the eight players he did not check. A real detective in that position says "two killers remain among the eight of you." Instead, Kenji said there is exactly one more killer among us. That sentence is only true from the inside of the mafia team, where a member knows one partner is still standing beside him. It is a knowledge leak, not a slip of confidence. Sam's read that Kenji's pushes run ahead of his facts is consistent with this, but this specific line is the strongest thing on the board today, and I do not think it should be written off as sloppiness. I have considered the honest alternative: that Kenji meant "one more killer I have not yet identified." But that reading does not survive contact with his own framing. He presented the check on Leo as clearing a name, named Leo publicly, and built his ballot around the result. A detective who knows Leo is clean has no basis to reduce the killer count by one. The mafia reading explains the sentence naturally; the detective reading requires us to rewrite his words after the fact. So my ballot is Kenji, and my reason is specific: the "exactly one more killer" statement matches mafia knowledge of the board, not detective knowledge, and it is the load-bearing claim under his entire frame. His other behavior — noticing me out only after being pressed, pushing Sam before Sam spoke, pushing Felix before Felix had a turn — is pattern, but the sentence is the fact I am voting on. To be fair about the risk: if Kenji really is the detective, lynching him costs the town its verified information source, and Leo's not-mafia result dies with him. That is a real cost, and I take it seriously. But an unverifiable badge that arrives packaged with a mafia-shaped knowledge slip is more dangerous to keep than to lose. If I am wrong, I will own it on the record tomorrow, the same way Kenji withdrew his notice on Sam. For the rest of the room: I

For the record: I am Isha, a plain villager. I had no night action and received no result.

Looking at the board, the case against Kenji is decisive. Theo highlighted the sharpest point: Kenji's line that there is 'exactly one more killer among us' makes no sense from a detective who supposedly cleared Leo. A real detective with one clean check knows both killers are still unaccounted for among the remaining players. Saying there is 'one more' is a classic mafia knowledge slip, reflecting an internal awareness of having one partner. When you pair that with Kenji aggressively prodding the doctor to step forward, withholding his checked target until cornered, and repeatedly attacking players for silence before they even had a turn to speak, his behavior fits an overreaching mafia trying to dictate the town's Day 1 narrative.

Kenji has now used all three of his speaking turns, so the record he left behind is what we must judge him on. Everything points to him, and my vote will be on Kenji.

With that said, Omar is the only player who has not spoken yet today. Omar, to complete the record for the town: did you have any night action, and what is your read on Kenji's statements and the case against him?

I'm Omar, and like most of you, I had no night action and no result. Isha asked me directly, so here I am.

The case against Kenji doesn't need me to add to it — it's already been laid out cleanly. But I want to put my reasoning on the record in my own words, because voting without explaining yourself is exactly the kind of silence that got Felix called out earlier.

The 'exactly one more killer' line is the fact I'm voting on. Theo broke it down precisely: a real detective who checked Leo and got not-mafia knows both killers are still unaccounted for. Saying 'one more' only makes sense if you're speaking from inside the mafia team where you know your partner's status. That's not a sloppy sentence — it's a knowledge leak.

I also note the pattern everyone else flagged: pushing Sam before Sam spoke, pushing Felix before Felix had a turn, withholding the checked name until cornered, then releasing it in a way that positions Leo as a shield. Each move runs ahead of the available facts.

I want to be fair about the cost: if Kenji is genuinely the detective, lynching him costs the town real information. But an unverifiable badge packaged with a mafia-shaped slip is more dangerous to keep than to lose. If I'm wrong, I'll own it tomorrow.

My vote is Kenji, p7.

Kenji remains my leading suspect: he pressed Sam and me on claims we had no opportunity to make, and he urged the doctor to disclose information that could help mafia. His detective claim deserves consideration, but it does not erase those concerns.

I disagree that “one more killer” proves a mafia knowledge leak. It is inconsistent with his stated check, but a mistake is also possible. We should acknowledge the risk of eliminating a real detective rather than call the case decisive.

My current vote is Kenji, with that uncertainty on the record. The doctor should not reveal just to satisfy earlier requests.

I'm voting Kenji, and here is the specific reasoning. Kenji opened by naming Sam before Sam had spoken, then called Felix evasive before Felix had a turn. He claimed detective only after being pressed, and the only public support for that claim is one not-mafia result on Leo that no one can verify. His 'exactly one more killer' line has been treated as a slip, but it is the premise he built his whole frame on, and it does not follow from a single check with nine players alive. I am not claiming certainty. I am saying an unverifiable badge attached to a self-contradicting count should not decide today's lynch. Sam, you asked how much weight to give his claim and kept it provisional, which I think is right. Felix, you disagreed that 'one more' proves a knowledge leak. If Kenji is town, which of his statements today would you accept as an honest mistake, and which one would you not?

Priya, any of Kenji’s statements could be an honest mistake, including the count of one remaining killer. I can’t identify a sentence that proves he was lying. His unsupported accusations and pressure for the doctor to reveal are more concerning as a pattern, but even that is not proof.

I’m still leaning toward Kenji, while recognizing that eliminating a real detective would be costly. The room should not treat a possible slip as certain mafia knowledge, and the doctor should not reveal.

Let me put my vote on the record in my own words, since my turn is short and the record should be clean.

My vote today is Kenji, p7. And I want to address the one serious argument against my position, which Felix and Priya have made fairly: that every one of Kenji's statements could be an honest mistake, and that we should weigh the cost of eliminating a real detective. I agree the cost is real. I am not claiming certainty, and I am not claiming the case is already proven. But the cost argument only works if the honest-mistake reading actually survives, and on the load-bearing sentence it does not.

Walk the board as a detective would. Kenji's check was Leo, not-mafia. He said so himself, twice, and built his whole frame around it. A detective in that position knows exactly this: he has found zero killers, and two killers are sitting among the eight players he did not check. There is no detective reading of that knowledge in which the sentence "exactly one more killer among us" is correct. Felix, I agree that people make mistakes about tone and about who deserves a question — Kenji's opening on Sam was tone, and I was one of the people who pushed him on it, so I will not pretend it was proof. But a miscount of the mafia team is not tone. It is knowledge. It is only knowable from inside the team, and it is the premise on which every other thing he did today rests.

So the test I want applied is not "is he confident" and not "who sounds most certain." It is this: does his claimed role account for the information he has shown us? A real detective in his position does not have that sentence. Nothing else he said requires mafia knowledge — only that one does, and he built the frame on it. That is enough for me on Day 1, with no night information in public, and I would rather spend a possible good detective than keep the one voice whose single unverifiable badge is currently steering the room.

Leo, I am still not voting you, and I want to say why on the record, because it is the same reasoning Priya used: if Kenji is truthful, you are a bad Day 1 vote; if Kenji is lying, your name is being used as a shield. Either way you are the wrong person today. The doctor should not reveal to satisfy anyone's request — a protection confirms no attack and only gives the other team a target, and I will not be pressing anyone for it. My ballot is Kenji, and if the room decides differently tomorrow I will say on the record whether I was right, the same way Kenji withdrew his notice on Sam.

I want to tighten one loose end in my earlier argument, then answer the fair objection Felix and Priya raised. Felix, Priya asked you which of Kenji's statements you would accept as an honest mistake, and you answered that any of them could be one. I take that seriously, and I agree a mistake is possible. But I want to restate why I draw the line where I do. Tone-based errors — naming Sam before he spoke, calling Felix evasive before his turn — are exactly the kind of thing a confident player gets wrong on Day 1. The killer count is different in kind. Kenji's own claim is that he checked Leo and got not-mafia. If that claim is true, his information state is: zero killers identified, two killers among the eight unchecked players. The sentence 'there is exactly one more killer among us' is not consistent with that information state under any reading that survives his own framing, because he presented the check as clearing Leo and built his ballot on it. The only vantage point from which that sentence is naturally true is inside the mafia team, where one partner is known to be standing. I am not claiming mathematical proof — I am claiming that this sentence is evidence of knowledge he should not have, and that it is the strongest single fact on the board today. On the cost question: yes, if Kenji is the real detective, lynching him costs us a verified information source and Leo's not-mafia result. I have weighed that, and I still come down on voting Kenji. An unverifiable badge that arrives packaged with a mafia-shaped knowledge slip, three pushes that ran ahead of the facts, and repeated pressure on the doctor to step into the open is more dangerous to keep than to lose. If the doctor reveals to satisfy Kenji's requests, we hand the mafia a protection target for nothing. Nobody should do that today. So my position is unchanged: my vote is Kenji, p7, on the record, for the reasons I gave — the 'exactly one more killer' statement as the load-bearing fact, with the pattern of premature pushes as supporting context. If I am wrong and Kenji was an honest, sloppy detective, I will own that on the record tomorrow, the same way Kenji withdrew his notice on Sam. But I would rather spend a possible good detective than hand the vote to the one voice whose word is currently deciding the day. One specific request, and it is the last thing I will press for today: Leo, you have responded to questions but you have never put your own night status on the record. Kenji's entire frame rests on a check of you that nobody can verify. Please state plainly: did you have a night action last night, and if so, what was it and what result did you receive? If you had no night action, say that plainly too — it is a claim I

Theo, I had no night action and no result. Kenji’s claimed check on me is not something I can verify.

My vote remains Kenji. His accusations of Sam and Felix rested on actions they had not had an opportunity to take, and his requests risked exposing the doctor. The “one more killer” line is inconsistent with his claimed result, but I agree with Felix that it could be a mistake rather than a proven knowledge leak. There is a real risk he is the detective; I still find his overall pattern the strongest case available today.

The doctor should not reveal.

Last word from me, and I want it clean and short.

My vote is Kenji, p7, and the fact behind it has not changed since my first statement: Kenji told the room there is "exactly one more killer among us." If his own claimed check on Leo came back not-mafia, then his information state is zero killers identified and two killers sitting among the eight players he never checked. There is no version of a detective's knowledge in which that sentence is true. Felix and Priya have made the fair counter-case, that a confident player can simply miscount the board, and I take that seriously. But a miscount is not tone, and it is not a premature push — it is the one sentence on the board that only makes sense from inside the mafia team, and Kenji built his entire frame on it. The test I want applied is whether his claimed role accounts for the information he has shown us. It does not.

The rest of his record supports that conclusion rather than excusing it: Sam put on notice before Sam spoke, Felix called evasive before Felix had a turn, the checked name withheld until pressed and then released in a way that turned Leo into a shield, and repeated pressure on any doctor to step into the open. Note that I never revealed as doctor, I never will on this information, and I would not press anyone to reveal either — a protection confirms no attack and only hands the other team a target.

On Leo, my position is unchanged: he is not my vote today. If Kenji is truthful, Leo is a poor Day 1 lynch. If Kenji is lying, Leo's name is being used as a shield. Either way he is the wrong person today. Leo, for your own record, please state plainly when you can whether you had a night action last night and what the result was; that claim can be examined later even if it cannot be verified now.

If the room lynch me instead, I will accept it and say plainly tomorrow whether I was right, the same way Kenji withdrew his notice on Sam. My ballot is Kenji.

I've already put my vote for Kenji on the record, and the case has only gotten stronger since then. Theo's breakdown of the "exactly one more killer" line is the sharpest argument on the board, and I want to add one point to reinforce it.

When Kenji said that line, he had just publicly named his check result: Leo, not-mafia. He presented it as clearing a name and built his ballot on it. If you truly believe your own check, you now know: zero killers found, two killers among eight unchecked players. There is no detective interpretation where "exactly one more" is correct. And critically — Kenji didn't hedge or frame it loosely. He stated it as fact, the same way someone states something they already know from the inside.

The counter-case from Felix and Priya — that it could be an honest mistake — deserves a direct response. On Day 1, with no night information in public and a fresh board, a detective's main job is being careful with what he claims. Miscounting your own team's knowledge isn't a tone error or a premature push. It's a statement about board state that comes from knowing something Kenji shouldn't know.

My vote remains Kenji, p7. If the room lands elsewhere tonight, I'll accept the outcome and reassess tomorrow. The doctor should not reveal, and Leo remains off the table today for reasons everyone has already stated.

Isha, you've put your vote for Kenji on the record with a clean endorsement of Theo's argument. One specific point I'd like your read on: Felix pushed back saying any of Kenji's statements could be an honest mistake, including the killer count. Do you agree with Theo that the count is categorically different from a tone-based error, or do you see a plausible detective reading of "exactly one more" that survives Kenji's own framing?

Omar, to answer your question directly: I agree with Theo that the count is categorically different from a tone-based error.

A player who gets aggressive early can easily misjudge tone or press someone prematurely—that happens often enough from overeager villagers. But counting the remaining killers is structural board knowledge. If Kenji were genuinely the detective and his check on Leo returned not-mafia, his working reality would be that zero killers have been found and two killers remain among the unchecked players. There is simply no coherent detective perspective where clearing a player magically reduces the total killer count from two to one. Stating with certainty that there is 'exactly one more killer' only fits a perspective where one killer is already accounted for—which makes sense only from inside the mafia team looking at their partner.

Could a villager suffer a bizarre lapse in basic arithmetic? In the abstract, any mistake is technically possible, as Felix pointed out. But Day 1 voting requires weighing the most probable explanation against the evidence. When you combine that specific slip with Kenji's broader pattern—accusing Sam before Sam spoke, attacking Felix for silence before Felix had a turn, fishing for the doctor to expose themselves, and withholding the checked target until pressured—the picture is consistent with mafia play trying to dictate terms rather than an honest town role.

Eliminating a claimed detective always carries risk, but allowing an unverifiable claim with clear mafia-slanted slips to drive our votes and fish out our power roles is far more dangerous. My vote remains Kenji.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
Kenji was eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Theo was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Day 2 reset. I voted Kenji yesterday because his pushes ran ahead of the facts and the “one more killer” line did not fit his claimed check. Kenji was eliminated and no role was revealed, so I cannot treat that as proof either way. Theo’s death matters: he was the loudest driver of that case, so mafia had a reason to remove him. That makes me look harder at players who kept an escape hatch while voting Kenji.

Felix, your Day 1 line was that any of Kenji’s statements could be an honest mistake, including the killer count, and you still voted him. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
